| Lead-in chamfer angle | **15–20°** | Published table is for FEP/PFA-encapsulated O-rings; it is conservative guidance rather than an FKM-specific requirement. All edges should be rounded and burr-free. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) |
| Minimum chamfer length — 3.53 mm cross-section | **1.8 mm at 15°; 1.4 mm at 20°** | Encapsulated-ring guidance; validate against the actual spigot, bore, squeeze, and FKM compound. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) |
| Minimum chamfer length — 1.78 mm cross-section | **1.1 mm at 15°; 0.9 mm at 20°** | Encapsulated-ring guidance; small FKM rings remain vulnerable to shaving and pinching at sharp transitions. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) |
| Recommended initial compression — static | **13–36% axial; 10–35% radial** | General guide ranges depend on cross-section and gland geometry; use ISO 3601-2 or the seal supplier’s compound-specific design table for final dimensions. (pqac-00000047) |
| Recommended initial compression — dynamic | **6–27% radial** | General guide range; the appropriate value depends on service, friction, lubrication, section size, and hardness. (pqac-00000047) |
| Maximum groove fill | **≤85%** | Leaves allowance for tolerances, thermal expansion, and fluid-induced swelling. (pqac-00000047) |
| Vacuum/argon-compatible assembly lubricant | **Very thin film of vacuum-grade PFPE**, such as an approved Fomblin- or Krytox-type grease | **Industry-standard engineering recommendation / author estimate; not established by the retrieved papers.** Argon is inert, but vacuum outgassing, powder contamination, cleaning chemistry, and the exact FKM compound must be checked. Obtain approval from the seal and lubricant suppliers; avoid ordinary hydrocarbon or silicone grease where chamber cleanliness is critical. |
| Permissible dwell time while temporarily stretched | **No defensible universal published limit found** | Do not use elongation-at-break as a dwell limit. **Engineering recommendation / estimate:** expand only during installation, preferably for seconds rather than minutes; release immediately and allow recovery before inspection or mating. Qualify the actual stretch–time combination with dimensional-recovery and leak tests. (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055) |


*Table: Summary of published FKM/O-ring design and installation limits, with caveats where guidance applies to encapsulated rings or generic elastomers. Lubricant and stretched-dwell recommendations are explicitly identified as industry practice or engineering estimates.*

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

Given a list of text names, read their contents.

but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - TERMINATED: Study terminated

        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

info.name: update_plan

strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)

Use the tools to answer the question: We want to check whether two collaborative robot arms (Universal Robots UR12e, the renamed UR10e: 12.5 kg payload, 1300 mm reach, +-0.05 mm repeatability, built-in force/torque sensing) on mobile bases could assemble a small laser powder bed fusion machine, including fitting its elastomer seals. The seals are FKM (Viton) 75A O-rings: (a) face glands, including a 3.53 mm cross-section O-ring in a rectangular groove about 300 x 210 mm around a chamber top (a molded AS568-2xx ring forced into a near-rectangular path), 1.78 mm rings in half-dovetail grooves on a vertical door and a sliding drawer; (b) a radial O-ring (AS568 2-238) in an external groove on a 96 mm spigot that slides into a bore; (c) two AS568 2-114 rings in internal grooves of a rod gland, through which a 16 mm rod is inserted; (d) small O-rings under KF flanges and sensor ports.

Please summarise, with sources: published work and industrial practice on automated and robotic O-ring and gasket installation (single-arm and dual-arm; special end effectors such as expanding cones, sleeves, fingers that roll the ring, mandrels, push-in tools for dovetail grooves; vision and force/torque checks for twist, roll-out, pinching and nicking), the stretch and compression limits during installation for FKM (percentage stretch at assembly, how long a ring can stay stretched, recommended lead-in chamfers and lubricants compatible with vacuum and argon), how success is verified (vision, leak test, force signature), typical cycle times and failure rates, and the hardest cases (large rings in long rectangular face grooves, dovetail grooves, internal grooves). Also: what dual-arm cobot assembly of small mechanical assemblies (screw driving with M3 to M6 screws, inserts, dowel pins, peg-in-hole at H7/g6) has achieved, the screwdriving end effectors used with UR arms (torque range), and where people still do it by hand. Abstract:
Assembly tasks executed by a robot have been studied broadly. Robot assembly applications in industry are achievable by a well-structured environment, where the parts to be assembled are located in the working space by fixtures. Recent changes in manufacturing requirements, due to unpredictable demanded products, push the factories to seek new smart solutions that can autonomously recover from failure conditions. In this way, new dual arm robot systems have been studied to design and explore applications based on its dexterity. It promises the possibility to get rid of fixtures in assembly tasks, but using less fixtures increases the uncertainty on the location of the components in the working space. It also increases the possibility of collisions during the assembly sequence. Under these considerations, adding perception such as force/torque sensors have been done to produce useful data to perform control actions. Unfortunately, the interaction forces between mating parts produced non-linear behavior. Consequently, machine learning algorithms have been considered an alternative tool to avoid the non-linearity. In this work we introduce an assembly strategy for an industrial dual arm robot based on the combination of a discrete event controller and Deep Neural Networks (DNN) to solve the peg-in-hole assembly. Our results show the difference between the use of DNN with one and with two force/torque sensors during the assembly task and demonstrate a 30% increase in the assembly success ratio when using a double force/torque sensor.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As the demands for assembly quality and efficiency increase, robot-assisted assembly applications are becoming more widespread. Peg-in-hole assembly, as a typical form of assembly, has been widely researched by scholars. Currently, robotic peg-in-hole assembly faces challenges such as complex analysis of part contact forces, difficulties in task modeling, and the failure of traditional strategies. Simply controlling the position of the robot's end effector cannot achieve high precision, high efficiency peg-in-hole assembly. Flexible assembly, especially intelligent flexible assembly, is becoming the future development trend. So there is a lack of comprehensive reviews on robotic flexible peg-in-hole assembly. This paper first outlines the basic components of peg-in-hole assembly and summarizes the two basic operational processes of peg-in-hole assembly, along with their related theoretical foundations. We then review and analyze the research on passive compliant assembly, active compliant assembly, and intelligent flexible assembly. Finally, it presents an outlook on the future development directions of robotic peg-in-hole assembly.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Disassembly is a core procedure in remanufacturing. Disassembly is currently carried out mainly by human operators. It is important to reduce the labor content of disassembly through automation, to make remanufacturing more economically attractive. Threaded fastener removal is one of the most difficult disassembly tasks to be fully automated. This article presents a new method developed for automating the unfastening of screws. An electric nutrunner spindle with a geared offset adapter was fitted to the end of a collaborative robot. The position of a hexagonal headed screw in a fitted stage was known only approximately, and its orientation in the hole was unknown. The robot was programed to perform a spiral search motion to engage the tool onto the screw. A control strategy combining torque and position monitoring with active compliance was implemented. An existing robot cell was modified and utilized to demonstrate the concept and to assess the feasibility of the solution using a turbocharger as a disassembly case study. Note to Practitioners—Remanufacturing is known to generate substantial economic, social, and environmental benefits. Disassembly is the first operation in a remanufacturing process chain. Unfastening threaded parts (“unscrewing”) is a common disassembly task accounting for approximately 40% of all disassembly activity. Like other disassembly tasks, often, unscrewing has to be carried out manually in remanufacturing due to difficulties caused by the variable and unpredictable condition of the end-of-life (EoL) products to be remanufactured. Automating unscrewing operations should reduce the labor content of disassembly, thus lowering remanufacturing costs and promoting the adoption of remanufacturing. This article proposes the use of a collaborative robot to perform autonomous unfastening of hexagonal headed screws. Collaborative robots have built-in force sensors and can be programed to carry out operations involving not only position but also active force and compliance control. They can work safely alongside human operators, enabling the latter to focus on jobs requiring high cognitive or manipulation abilities. The article presents a novel spiral search technique developed to improve the rate of successful engagement between the robot end effector and the screw heads despite uncertainties in the location of the screws. The technique was successfully demonstrated on the dismantling of a turbocharger but can readily be applied to other EoL products with hexagonal headed screws. It can also be used with other kinds of screws (e.g., Phillips screws and slotted-head screws) simply by changing the tool and tuning the robot control parameters. A limitation of the proposed technique is that it can only deal reliably with undamaged screws. In our future research, we will consider screws that are in imperfect conditions through usage and develop appropriate solutions for their removal by robots.

Abstract:
Manufacturers of hydraulic fluids invest a lot of effort and resources in improving their physico-chemical properties, with the goal of getting as close as possible to the properties of an ideal hydraulic fluid. It should be non- flammable, environmentally friendly, sustainable and should have excellent physical and chemical properties. After decades of development in the field of ionic liquids and the search for an ionic liquid suitable for use in hydraulic systems, ionic hydraulic liquids are now already in industrial use, especially on devices that operate in harsh and risky operating conditions. Since ionic hydraulic fluids are a completely new type of hydraulic fluid, one of the issues is their compatibility with the materials present in the hydraulic components, including all the seals. This paper refers to the process of testing the compatibility of hydraulic seal materials with different types of ionic hydraulic fluids according to the standardized percentages and recommendations, with emphasis on changes in the swell, shrinkage and hardness of the seals. The presented results are a useful guide for selecting suitable seal materials in case of using high-tech ionic hydraulic fluids.

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Rubber O‐rings are vital sealing components in petrochemical and refinery applications, where reliable performance under harsh conditions is essential. This study employs a multianalytical approach to investigate the material composition, curing system, and performance of an industrial O‐ring. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy identified characteristic bands at 1394 cm
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , confirming the O‐ring as a fluorocarbon elastomer (FKM), with a peak at 3428 cm
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    (attributed to N–H groups) diminishing post‐Soxhlet extraction, indicating an amine‐based curing system. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) revealed a 91.69% weight loss up to 700°C, with significant degradation at 493°C (58.37% loss between 400 and 550°C) and a residual mass of 8.31%, suggesting minimal filler content. Mechanical testing demonstrated a modulus of 4.60 MPa, tensile strength of 5.86 MPa, strain at break of 165%, and a compression set of 41%, reflecting robust material properties. The O‐ring was identified as Viton A (a vinylidene fluoride [VDF]/hexafluoropropylene [HFP] copolymer) with a diamine curing system, typical of early FKM grades used in demanding chemical environments. While FTIR identifies key functional groups, its integration with TGA (for thermal stability and filler content), Soxhlet extraction (for additive isolation), and mechanical testing provides a practical, accessible framework for reverse engineering industrial elastomers—offering actionable insights into material suitability for petrochemical sealing applications.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study investigates the pressure-dependent mechanical behavior and surface degradation of fluorocarbon elastomer (FKM, Viton®) O-ring seals following prolonged high-pressure hydrogen exposure. Specimens were aged at up to 7000 psi for 192 h and evaluated using tensile testing and optical image analysis. The results show a non-monotonic evolution of peak force, stiffness, and energy absorption, with increased load-bearing response at higher pressures accompanied by reduced displacement capacity. Normalized force–displacement behavior shows broadly similar loading profiles across pressure conditions; however, this representation is used for comparative visualization and does not establish preservation of the deformation mechanism. Image-based analysis reveals a significant increase in micro-defect density and surface heterogeneity with pressure, suggesting increased formation of surface micro-defects. These findings highlight pressure-dependent changes in polymer network response and surface morphology under hydrogen exposure. The study provides insights into structure–property relationships governing elastomer performance in hydrogen environments.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000000

From text 'monguzzi2022flexibleroboticstrategy pages 7-8'.

Andrea Monguzzi, Marco Maiocchi, Andrea Maria Zanchettin, and Paolo Rocco. Flexible robotic strategy for the assembly of ring-shaped elastic objects. Procedia Computer Science, 200:376-385, Jan 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2022.01.236, doi:10.1016/j.procs.2022.01.236. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes robotic O-ring installation as an enlargement-and-insertion process using a custom gripper fingertip equipped with pins. The strategy is experimentally validated for inserting HNBR O-rings onto piston grooves, including a UR5 gripper configuration. The algorithm designs one or more gripper steps based on O-ring and piston dimensions, pin radius, pin spacing, and fingertip height. The selected step must accommodate the elastic object’s radius and thickness while allowing insertion into the piston’s outer groove. The fingertip pins are positioned at the edge of a step, and their height is chosen slightly greater than the O-ring thickness. This geometry is intended to reduce pin bending during enlargement and improve positioning repeatability. For small O-rings, the two-pin fingertip arrangement can overlap and become infeasible; the proposed remedy is a triangular configuration in which the two fingertip pins are replaced by one pin. The excerpt does not mention expanding cones, mandrels, or push-in tools. It also does not explicitly report twist, roll-out, pinching, or nicking as observed failure modes. Instead, it identifies geometric interference/overlap, pin bending, improper contact sequencing, and contact between the fingertip base and the part as feasibility risks. Successful insertion assumes the piston groove contacts the elastic O-ring before contacting the pins.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'monguzzi2022flexibleroboticstrategy pages 8-10'.

Andrea Monguzzi, Marco Maiocchi, Andrea Maria Zanchettin, and Paolo Rocco. Flexible robotic strategy for the assembly of ring-shaped elastic objects. Procedia Computer Science, 200:376-385, Jan 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2022.01.236, doi:10.1016/j.procs.2022.01.236. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes robotic O-ring assembly using a UR5 collaborative robot fitted with a Camozzi CGZT three-jaw, double-effect pneumatic gripper and custom 3D-printed stepped fingertips. The O-ring is first grasped and deposited on the fixture. The gripper then expands the ring to a calculated configuration large enough for the piston to pass through from above. Once the piston groove reaches the O-ring’s height, the jaws close to a predefined position, and the robot lifts the piston so the ring becomes trapped in the groove. A pair of proportional pneumatic regulators controls jaw pressure and stroke; because the relationships between control input, pressure, actuation time, and stroke are linear, the required expansion time can be computed from the desired ring deformation. The design uses multiple contact points and stepped fingertips rather than a round C-shaped contact arrangement, allowing different O-ring sizes and other parts to be handled. The reported experiments achieved approximately 95% success, with failures or reduced reliability associated primarily with hand-positioning uncertainty, especially for smaller rings, rather than explicitly documented twist, roll-out, pinching, or nicking. Each complete cycle took approximately 30 seconds. No expanding cone, mandrel, or separate push-in tool is described; the expanding function is performed directly by the pneumatic jaws and custom fingertips.

TS SOlUTIONS. O-rings and back-up rings. Unknown journal, 2016.

The excerpt provides general guidance for automated O-ring installation but does not identify particular robotic end effectors, gripper designs, expanding cones, or push-in tools. It emphasizes that automation requires careful preparation, including surface treatments such as Flexcoat™ to reduce installation forces and eliminate stick effects, thereby making removal easier. Dimensionally unstable O-rings require experienced handling, specialized packing, and preparation for reliable automatic installation. For manual or assisted assembly, tools should have no sharp edges, installation aids should be used where possible, and the O-ring must not be twisted. O-rings should not be overstretched, and an assembly mandrel made from soft metal or burr-free plastic is essential when installation over threads, splines, or keyways cannot be avoided. The design should minimize passage over edges or bores; lead-in chamfers, deburred bores, rounded edges, and removal of chips or foreign particles are recommended. The passage does not explicitly discuss robotic failure modes such as roll-out, pinching, or nicking, but its warnings about twisting, sharp edges, burrs, installation forces, and difficult geometries indicate the types of handling risks that automated equipment must control.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT To support shifting to high mix/low volume production, manufacturers in high wage countries aim for robotizing their production operations – with a special focus on the late production phases, where robotic assembly cells are then confronted with any complexities resulting from part and product varieties. The ‘World Robot Challenge 2018’ (WRC 2018) emulated such high mix/low volume production scenarios in a competition taking place in Tokyo, Japan. As part of our activities in SDU's newly founded I4.0 Lab, we integrated and advanced our experiences and developments from our various R & D projects in a novel robotic assembly cell design to compete in the WRC 2018. This article describes the system architecture as well as main aspects of its implementation regarding robot control, robot programming and computer vision and how they contributed to winning the challenge. Due to the application of collaborative robots, the cell design allows for operation without fences. Hence, multiple copies of the cell can be arranged in a highly reconfigurable, highly adaptable matrix structure in which several production flows can be handled concurrently. This concept was demonstrated by the installation of a duplicate cell that allowed for parallel developments on two cells and prolonged development also after shipping the first cell to Japan. Abstract:
A collaborative robot, or cobot, enables users to work closely with it through direct communication without the use of traditional barricades. Cobots eliminate the gap that has historically existed between industrial robots and humans while they work within fences. Cobots can be used for a variety of tasks, from communication robots in public areas and logistic or supply chain robots that move materials inside a building, to articulated or industrial robots that assist in automating tasks which are not ergonomically sound, such as assisting individuals in carrying large parts, or assembly lines. Human faith in collaboration has increased through human–robot collaboration applications built with dependability and safety in mind, which also enhances employee performance and working circumstances. Artificial intelligence and cobots are becoming more accessible due to advanced technology and new processor generations. Cobots are now being changed from science fiction to science through machine learning. They can quickly respond to change, decrease expenses, and enhance user experience. In order to identify the existing and potential expanding role of artificial intelligence in cobots for industrial applications, this paper provides a systematic literature review of the latest research publications between 2018 and 2022. It concludes by discussing various difficulties in current industrial collaborative robots and provides direction for future research.

Abstract:

 Over the past few decades, collaborative robots (cobots) have emerged as a key element in the advancement of smart industries and the transition to Industry 5.0, facilitating operations alongside human workers to reduce both cognitive and physical strain. Cobots have primarily been used for tasks such as material handling, assembly and precise positioning, but their integration into quality control and inspection remains underexplored. Using a mixed-methods approach, this paper conducts a thorough investigation of current applications of cobots in quality assurance, both in academic research and in industrial practice. Through a systematic review of the academic literature and analysis of real-world industrial case studies, the paper examines the current state and potential advances in manufacturing quality control facilitated by cobots. The findings suggest that while cobots are currently being used primarily to improve efficiency through in-process visual inspection, there are significant barriers to their widespread adoption in quality control. These barriers include high initial costs, lack of technical expertise among workers, integration challenges with existing systems, data security concerns and regulatory compliance issues. Nevertheless, the potential for research and industrial growth through the use of cobots in quality control is considerable. By drawing on insights from academic research and practical implementations, this study provides researchers, practitioners and policy makers with a comprehensive perspective on the innovative use of cobots to improve quality control in manufacturing.

## pqac-00000005

From text 'solutions2016oringsandbackup pages 50-52'.

TS SOlUTIONS. O-rings and back-up rings. Unknown journal, 2016.

The excerpt provides O-ring installation stretch and interference guidance, but it does not specify how long an O-ring may remain stretched, a lead-in chamfer angle or dimensions, or a lubricant compatible with vacuum and argon for FKM/Viton seals. For piston (outer) sealing, the nominal inside diameter should be stretched 2–5% in dynamic applications and 2–8% in static applications. For dynamic service, maximum stretch should remain at or below 5% because excessive elongation reduces cross section and may impair service life. For rod (inner) sealing, the O-ring outside diameter should be at least equal to the groove outside diameter; recommended maximum outside interference is 3% for O-rings larger than 250 mm diameter and 5% for smaller O-rings. The text warns that exceeding interference limits can increase cross section and affect service life. For static axial sealing, external pressure calls for the O-ring inside diameter to be approximately 1–3% smaller than the inner groove diameter, while internal pressure calls for the O-ring outside diameter to be equal to or up to 1–2% larger than the outer groove diameter. It also notes that small O-rings may require wider tolerances.

## pqac-00000011

From text 'brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 102-106'.

G Brera. Collaborative screwdriving: integrating robot optimal sequence algorithms for increased efficiency. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt describes a collaborative screwdriving system using a cobot and an optimized TSP-based screwing sequence. Aligning all screwing points with the same orientation improved cycle time by 30.34% and reduced computation time by a factor of 218 compared with allowing separate point orientations. The optimized sequence itself achieved a 9.81% cycle-time reduction compared with manually or visually generated screwing sequences. The TSP implementation was reported to deliver solutions within a fraction of a second, supporting real-time collaborative operation. The collaborative application used vision-system data to identify screw locations, track the cobot head, detect the operator’s hands, and adapt the cobot’s action sequence and speed. A trial involving five individuals produced positive evaluations of usefulness, support, overall performance, usability, and reduced mental and physical demands. However, this excerpt does not specify the screwdriving end effector used with UR robot arms, torque ranges for M3, M4, M5, or M6 screws, or a numerical screwdriving success rate. The five-person trial reports favorable user outcomes but is not a quantified task success-rate measurement.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 31-35'.

G Brera. Collaborative screwdriving: integrating robot optimal sequence algorithms for increased efficiency. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt provides general information about screwdriving end-effector and feeding strategies, but it does not specifically discuss UR robot arms. Screw pickup can be performed using magnetic attraction, vacuum suction, or mechanical grasping. Vacuum grippers offer precise orientation control and support a broader range of screw materials, although they require extra components such as a pump, valve, tubing, and adapter; the adapter may be bulky in confined spaces. Blow feeding instead orients and propels screws through a tube to the screwdriver tip, avoiding a separate pickup step and potentially improving throughput, though it is unsuitable for screws with low aspect ratios that may tumble in the tube. The excerpt does not report torque ranges for M3, M4, M5, or M6 screws, nor does it give a collaborative robot screwdriving cycle time or a process success rate. It mentions that various fault-detection methods achieve recognition rates around 90% or higher, including an example of 97%, but this refers to failure-mode recognition rather than overall screwdriving success. It also states that conventional automation deployment commonly takes 8–17 weeks, which is not a cycle-time measurement.

Abstract:
In Gasket Assembly, a deformable gasket must be aligned and pressed into a narrow channel. This task is common for sealing surfaces in the manufacturing of automobiles, appliances, electronics, and other products. Gasket Assembly is a long-horizon, high-precision task and the gasket must align with the channel and be fully pressed in to achieve a secure fit. To compare approaches, we present 4 methods for Gasket Assembly: one policy from deep imitation learning and three procedural algorithms. We evaluate these methods with 100 physical trials. Results suggest that the Binary+ algorithm succeeds in 10/10 on the straight channel whereas the learned policy based on 250 human teleoperated demonstrations succeeds in 8/10 trials and is significantly slower. Code, CAD models, videos, and data can be found at https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/robot-gasket/.

Abstract:
Grasping deformable objects remains a challenging operational task for robots in diverse industrial applications. Different characteristics of deformable objects to be gripped need to be considered in the mechanical design of the gripper. Mechanical grippers often rely on sensors and appropriate control strategies to grasp deformable objects. This study classifies deformable objects, grippers and gripper manufacturers, and their corresponding gripping strategies. In the study of control strategies, model-based algorithm control strategies are often ineffective as often the objects to be gripped are unknown in terms of its rigidity and other morphological characteristics. In contrast, model-free algorithms do not need parametric information of the objects as only input-output signal is required. This allows the model-free controlled grippers adapt to diverse and unstructured environments. Finally, the advantages and disadvantages of current deformable object-grasping techniques are discussed and summarized. The challenges and future directions of robots grasping deformable objects are pointed out.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of robotic hand designs from the perspective of precision grasping. The review analyzes key aspects of mechanical architecture, including finger kinematic structures, actuation and transmission systems, structural materials and fabrication methods, mechanical intelligence, and control-oriented mechanical design. Different design strategies such as fully actuated fingers, underactuated mechanisms, tendon-driven systems, linkage-based architectures, and soft robotic structures are compared in terms of dexterity, adaptability, accuracy, and system complexity. The analysis highlights several important trends, including the transition toward compliant and bio-inspired mechanisms, the integration of lightweight materials and additive manufacturing, and the increasing role of sensor–structure integration for precise force and position control. Despite significant progress, challenges such as friction, hysteresis, transmission compliance, and limited integration space still affect grasping accuracy and reliability. Based on the reviewed literature, future research should focus on hybrid actuation strategies, bio-inspired structural design, graded material architectures with structurally integrated sensing, and modular platforms to improve precision manipulation and system robustness in next-generation robotic hands.</jats:p>

The excerpt describes an automated deformable gasket (HNBR O-ring) assembly process using a UR5 collaborative robot equipped with a Camozzi pneumatic three-jaw gripper and custom 3D-printed fingertips. The O-ring is first grasped and placed in the fixture, then enlarged by opening the gripper jaws sufficiently to permit the piston to enter from above. After the piston’s groove reaches the O-ring height, the gripper jaws close to a predefined configuration, allowing the O-ring to contract around the piston. Jaw opening and closing times are calculated according to the required O-ring deformation, using the linear relationship between regulator control and gripper stroke. Repeated experiments achieved an approximately 95% success rate, despite manually positioning each O-ring. Smaller O-rings were more sensitive to initial placement uncertainty. Abstract:

 In this paper we present the re-engineering process of an assembly line that features speed reducers and multipliers for agricultural applications. The product operates as an interface between an input torque, typically supplied by an agricultural vehicle, and an output torque, generally moving specific equipment placed on a trolley equipped with a tow hook. The "as-is'' (initial version) line was highly inefficient due to several critical issues, including the high age of the machines, a non-optimal arrangement of them in the shop floor, and the absence of controls and process standards. These critical issues were analysed with the tools offered by Lean Manufacturing, which made it possible to identify irregularities and operations that require effort (Mura), overload (Muri), and waste (Muda). The definition of the "to-be'' (new version) assembly line included actions to update the department layout, to modify the assembly process and to design the line feeding system in compliance with the well-known concepts of Golden Zone and Strike Zone. The whole process addressed, in particular, the problem of the incorrect assembly of the oil seals. The registered error was mainly caused by the difficulty in visually identifying the correct side of the assembled oil seal, and by the mental fatigue of operators at the end of the shift. The solution studied in this paper resulted in a Poka-Yoke solution, which, leveraging the modern technologies and methods of deep learning and computer vision, monitors the process flow of the operators through a camera, preventing its completion in the event of an assembly error.

Matteo Martinelli, Marco Lippi, and Rita Gamberini. Poka yoke meets deep learning: a proof of concept for an assembly line application. Applied Sciences, 12:11071, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/app122111071, doi:10.3390/app122111071. This article has 63 citations.

The excerpt describes a camera-based poka-yoke system for verifying oil-seal positioning during crankcase assembly. A camera mounted beneath the press arm observes the seal before bearing insertion and must distinguish a correctly oriented seal, an upside-down seal, and a missing seal. The inspection is required to handle variation in seal position, including crooked or nonparallel placement, and changing viewpoints as the camera moves with the press head. Press descent is permitted only when the vision system confirms correct pre-positioning, allowing the controller to prevent assembly errors. The method uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) for three-class image classification. The dataset contains 500 smartphone-captured full-HD images of a crankcase and oil seal, covering the three configurations. Images were resized to 240 × 320 pixels, converted to grayscale, and processed with a 5 × 5 high-pass filter to emphasize borders and high-frequency information. The compact CNN uses one convolutional layer with 32 3 × 3 filters, max pooling, a 64-neuron dense layer, dropout, and a three-neuron output layer, trained using Adam and categorical cross-entropy. The excerpt does not address twisted, spiral, pinched, or nicked O-rings, nor force-signature analysis, although it notes that force selection could potentially be automated based on the detected component.

The assembly-line analysis identified leakage of a speed increaser around the shaft as a recurring quality problem. Customer-return inspections showed that the failures resulted from oil seals being mounted upside down. The existing compressed-air test could reliably detect a missing seal but did not guarantee detection of leakage caused by an inverted seal, and testing occurred only after the product was closed. Consequently, correcting an incorrectly positioned seal required difficult and costly disassembly, including bearing extraction with specialized tools, substantial force, and skilled labor. The proposed solution was intended to monitor the seal at the assembly location, before bearing insertion, using Poka Yoke combined with deep learning. This timing was considered essential because inspection must occur simultaneously with assembly; otherwise, an operator could install or omit the seal after the check. The uniformly black seals, small dimensions, inadequate lighting, and operator fatigue made visual discrimination difficult and prone to error. Andrea Monguzzi, Marco Maiocchi, Andrea Maria Zanchettin, and Paolo Rocco. Flexible robotic strategy for the assembly of ring-shaped elastic objects. Procedia Computer Science, 200:376-385, Jan 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2022.01.236, doi:10.1016/j.procs.2022.01.236. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt is highly relevant to an automated collaborative-robot O-ring assembly station. It presents a flexible robotic strategy for inserting ring-shaped elastic objects, including O-rings, into outer grooves on rigid parts. The system is designed for different ring sizes and stiffnesses and uses a generic robot, a simple actuated fixture, and a generic gripper rather than specialized tooling or additional sensors. The robot’s responsibilities are limited to picking and placing the elastic seals and manipulating the rigid components, while the fixture performs the more complex deformation and insertion actions in synchronization with the robot. The approach is intended for flexible, reprogrammable manufacturing with multiple product variants and is described as less expensive than specialized insertion machines. Automotive applications specifically include engine, fuel-system, air-conditioning, and transmission components requiring seals against oil, fuel, or air. The excerpt does not describe a lubricator or lubricant dispenser, nor does it provide detailed information about a dedicated O-ring feeder, dispensing hardware, cycle times, or a complete production-line layout. It does, however, support the concept of a cobot-based O-ring pick-and-place and insertion station using a synchronized fixture and no additional sensing.

Abstract:
Automating the extraction of mechanical fasteners from end-of-life (EOL) electronic waste is challenging due to unpredictable conditions and unknown fastener locations relative to robotic coordinates. This study develops a system for extracting cross-recessed screws using a Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) for screw detection, integrated with industrial robot simulation software. The simulation models the tooling, camera, environment, and robot kinematics, enabling real-time control and feedback between the robot and the simulation environment. The system, tested on a robotic platform with custom tooling, including force and torque sensors, aimed to optimize fastener removal. Key performance indicators included the speed and success rate of screw extraction, with success rates ranging from 78 to 89% on the first pass and 100% on the second. The system uses a state-based program design for fastener extraction, with real-time control via a web-socket interface. Despite its potential, the system faces limitations, such as longer cycle times, with single fastener extraction taking over 30 s. These challenges can be mitigated by refining the tooling, DCNN model, and control logic for improved efficiency.

Abstract:
Integrating robot systems into manufacturing lines is a time-consuming process. In the era of digitalization, the research and development of new technologies is crucial for improving integration processes. Numerous challenges, including the lack of standardization, as well as intricate stakeholder relationships, complicate the process of robotic systems integration. This process typically consists of acquisition, integration, and deployment of the robot systems. This thesis focuses on three areas that help automate and simplify robotic systems integration. In the first area, related to acquisition, a constraint-based configurator is demonstrated that resolves compatibility challenges between robot devices, and automates the configuration process. This reduces the risk of integrating incompatible devices and decreases the need for experts during the configuration phase. In the second area, related to integration, the interoperable modeling format, Unified Robot Description Format (URDF), is investigated, where a detailed analysis is performed, revealing significant inconsistencies and critical improvements. This format is widely used for kinematic modeling and 3D visualization of robots, and its models can be reused across simulation tools. Improving this format benefits a wide range of users, including robotics engineers, researchers, and students. In the third area, related to deployment, Digital Twins (DTs) for robot systems are explored, as these improve efficiency and reduce downtime. A comprehensive literature review of DTs is conducted, and a case study of modular robot systems is developed. This research can accelerate the adoption of DTs in the robotics industry. These insights and approaches improve the process of robotic systems integration, offering valuable contributions that future research can build upon, ultimately driving efficiency, and reducing costs.

G Brera. Collaborative screwdriving: integrating robot optimal sequence algorithms for increased efficiency. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt provides general information relevant to integrating a screwdriving end effector with a Universal Robots collaborative robot, but it does not give detailed specifications for OnRobot, Robotiq, Atlas Copco, or Kolver screwdrivers. It identifies automated screw feeding with a handheld nutrunner as one automation configuration: a screw feeder continuously supplies screws to the nutrunner while the operator applies torque. It also describes robotic screwdriving as combining manual-like flexibility with the consistency of conventional automation. The excerpt directly describes a collaborative robot assembly cell using two Universal Robots UR10e robots, each with six degrees of freedom, a 1.3 m reach, and a 10 kg load capacity. One robot is equipped with a Weiss Robotics WSG50 gripper, while the other uses a Robotiq 2F85 gripper and a Desoutter ECSF16 screwdriver. The ECSF16 supports programmable torque and velocity profiles, making it relevant to automated screwdriving and screw insertion processes. The system also uses specialized 3D-printed components mounted directly on the screwdriver bit to mechanically handle non-magnetic screws and create an interference lock between the screw head and bit. Custom printed fixtures and bit holders facilitate rapid tool exchange and flexible reconfiguration of screwing actions. The broader cell architecture includes overhead sensing, a reconfigurable worktable, and robot calibration procedures, but the excerpt does not provide details about UR+ certification, a specific certified-tool listing, or measured screwdriving performance. It therefore supports identification of the hardware and the general screw-handling approach, but not claims about UR+ certification or a complete cobot screw-insertion application specification.

     This paper discusses a method for flexible robot programming and execution control, through the enablement of human-robot
      collaborative tasks.  This method considers data that are initially generated, in an offline programming tool and are corrected
      online by considering feedback from force and vision sensors. A number of tasks are dynamically assigned to both human and
      robot resources. The user tests the programming result via an external control system. The initially assigned tasks can be re-
      assigned online.  The method has been implemented, at the top of ROS, as an android application and has been applied to

     1. Introduction

      The robot programming methods have been requiring time and expertise from the robot programmer. Expertise
     is required both on the task that is to be programmed and the robot controller’s architecture [1][2]. Taking into
    consideration the existence of several different programming languages (approximately one for each manufacturer)
    within the industrial robotics,  it  is obvious why robot programming  is accomplished only by expert robot
    programmers. Interaction with the robot and its programming has to be simplified in order to enable the wider use
    of robots, by motivating SMEs [1][4] to invest in robotics. Such activities lead to increasing the flexibility of the
    existing productions [3].
      The use of the CAD files for the required information is an active research topic [5][6]. Several industrial
    solutions, such as Delmia or Process Simulate, are offered for offline robot programming that can generate the
    robot’s motions even for a full production line. However, those tools require that the programmer specify the robot
    tasks even at a low level. Besides, the use of those tools requires expertise in robotics, since these solutions are
     difficult to be used by untrained operators. The operators must be typically trained for several weeks in order to
    learn how to use these interfaces. Even minor changes in the robot program require a significant programming
     effort.
      Another trend in the recent years, is the teaching of robotic programs through the observation of a human
    demonstration [7][8]. Such a kind of an approach relies on a predefined set of commands (speech of vision
    gestures) and the necessary sensors to grasp those commands [9]. The main disadvantage of these systems was that
    they do not provide any kind of interface for the human’s interaction with the generation of the robotic process.
     The current trend in order to overcome these obstacles focuses on task-level programming. In this case, the
   programming is based on a library of predefined lower-level building blocks [10][11]. Those blocks consist of
    sequences of motion primitives, which are encapsulated generic information for the generation of  the requested
     task. The operator still has to insert the low-level detail. However, since knowledge is quickly widespread, any
    knowledge gained is of an increasing importance to the intuitively teaching robots [12]. There exist several
    knowledge bases for enabling the definition of additional parameters [13][14].
    A recent report by the European Union on robotic applications identifies the human interaction as the key
    technology to research with high likelihood of being used in application [15][16]. Especially in the case of SMEs,
    the human robot cooperation is a promising concept that allows for increasing the automation level within the
    manufacturing processes and enabling the coexistence of both actors. Thus, the communication through human like
    natural interfaces increases. In terms of ergonomics, the main objectives of using natural communication channels
    are a shortening of both  training times and operating cycle times. Multimodality,  i.e., a use of multiple
    communication channels simultaneously or successively, plays an important role in the design of intuitive control
    systems. Scientific publications in the field of industrial robotics, e.g., [17][18][19], have shown that multimodal
    control systems are more efficient and user friendly than conventional systems are . The multimodal human robot
    interaction includes human like communication, which mostly consists in speech (auditory) and gestures (visual)
    [20].
      This paper proposes a method for flexible robot programming, through the use of a flexible programming
    process. The approach of the proposed method is presented in section 2, while the implementation follows in
    section 3. The application of the method, in several case studies,  is presented in section 4. Discussion and
    conclusions follow.

     2. Approach

      The method of the programming platform is based on the task oriented programming, thus, enabling the easier
   programming of industrial robot motions, with the use of user friendly interfaces. The specific structure of robot
   programming focuses on the necessary input data to the robot, rather than on low level details. The basic
    motivation of the this framework is visible in Fig.1 and focus has been given to:
    •  User friendly programming methods that would allow a non-expert user to easily program a robot.
    •  Offline generation of robot program.
    •  Dynamic update of the human- robot interface via friendly medians (e.g. tablets)
    •  Increase in the production rate by exploiting the synergy between humans and robots.
    •  Robotic cells that are quickly adaptable to frequently changing production scenarios.                          Stereos Alexandros Matthaiakis et al. / Procedia Manufacturing 11 (2017) 431 – 440                       433

•  Universal layout to support multiple applications.

dependent on each other, and there is a need for them to work together to make robotic

2.5  Potential Directions

This section describes some of the potential directions to work towards in order to reduce
the effect of the challenges described above.


2.5.1  Increase Interchangeability Through System Modularity

To decrease (re-)integration time, and improve re-usability of devices, it is crucial to work
towards modular robot systems, where devices can easily be exchanged. This can be achieved
by developing plug-and-play devices, or by defining and using standardized interfaces for the
devices in a robot system. Inspiration can be drawn from a successful system, the Personal
Computer (PC), which defines standards on interoperability including the responsibilities of
OEMs [39], and describes the usability of the computers by explicitly defining the vocab-
ulary to be used across operating systems [40].  If robot system modularity is improved in
the future, it will help robotic systems integration with all three issues mentioned above.
However, system modularity is out of the scope of this thesis.



                                       25                                                                2.5. POTENTIAL DIRECTIONS


2.5.2  Easier Robot System Configuration

Manually configuring the devices in a robot system and determining their compatibility can
take time, adding to the total integration costs. Developing a configurator that can automate
this process, similarly to the PC configurator5, may help customers and integrators easier
determine the compatibility of devices, when configuring a robot system.  This may also
lead to an increase in the reuse of devices, if their compatibility can easily be determined
in a configuration tool.  If a configurator is developed containing all the domain knowledge
about devices, it will be easier for new integrators to enter the market, and it will also
shorten the integration time of robot systems. This PhD project addresses this by creating a
proof-of-concept configurator, that takes into account some of the documentation challenges
described above, and is presented in chapter 3. RQ2 is addressed in this chapter, and can be
related to tackling challenges CH 2A by creating a configurator that takes these limitations
into account, CH 4A by enabling reuse of devices through automated configuration, CH 4C
by enabling a faster acquisition process, and I3 by providing a tool for finding appropriate
devices regardless of OEM restrictions.


2.5.3  Simulation and Digital Twins

To decrease the integration and deployment time of robot systems, the design can be simu-
lated and verified before investing in the hardware [17]. Simulation can be used in multiple
phases of integration and deployment. It can be used in the design phase to experiment with
different devices, or before deployment for system verification (as virtual commissioning),
or in the context of DTs where processes can be simulated and compared to data from the
physical system for optimization of the process.
   As simulations can be used across different phases of robotic systems integration, this
PhD project focuses on investigating and improving an interoperable format for modeling
devices and reusing these models across different simulation environments. This is presented
in chapter 4. RQ3 is addressed in this chapter, and can be related to tackling challenges
CH 1A by enabling faster simulation setup and therefore faster integration and less time for
discrepancies to occur, and I3 by improving interoperability across software tools.
   The concept of DTs in the context of unit level machines is explored and a case-study
is presented showing how a DS of a modular robot system can be developed. These are
introduced in chapter 5. RQ4 is addressed in this chapter.


2.5.4  Reduce Vendor Lock-in Through Interoperability

Creating interoperable devices and software for robotics is essential for tackling the negative
effects of vendor lock-in and mitigating the associated risks. The configurator presented in
chapter 3 allows defining rules for various types of devices, thus enabling configuration of
a larger database of devices, which may assist in reducing vendor lock-in. The modeling
format, URDF, presented in chapter 4, is an interoperable format that can be imported
into various simulation and visualization tools, making users less dependent on a single

This PhD thesis aims to reduce the time spent in the process on robotic systems integra-

3.1  Research Method

The goal of this chapter is to answer RQ2 that is defined as:  is it possible to define a
configurator of modular robot systems that takes application requirements and compatibility
of devices into account?
   To address RQ2, we present a domain model that tackles some of the documentation and
compatibility-related challenges presented above in section 2.4. A proof-of-concept of the
domain model is developed and validated on a small subset of products from an integrator’s
(Technicon’s) product catalog. As the goal of this research is to be applied in the industry,
we follow the technology transfer model defined by [41], as illustrated in fig. 3.1, where an

5.1.2  RoboDK Virtual Environment


An important tool extensively employed is the virtual simulation environment

within RoboDK. As illustrated in the flow diagram depicted in Chapter 3 (Figure

3.1), the initial step indeed involves constructing a RoboDK simulation inclusive

of all the station’s components.

   The initial simulation, which forms the basis for exploring various robot con-

figurations, consists of objects previously mentioned in the real-world bench

setup. The assembly of the Vention table is facilitated through the Vention web-

site’s Machine Builder module, allowing to assemble a station by selecting com-

ponents from the catalogue. Once the table is integrated into the simulation en-

vironment, the robot is precisely positioned equidistant from the left corner of

the table and aligned with the real-world orientation. This is accomplished by

configuring specific joint values for the robot and adjusting the orientation of the

robot’s base frame within the simulation. Subsequently, the TCP tool screwdriv-

ing CAD model is generated, imported, placed and oriented accordingly to the

real bench configuration. The individual assembly components are easily placed

in their exact real-world positions, being designed to seamlessly match the Ven-

tion plate pattern and threaded holes. Recognizing the importance of flexibility,

each component of the assembly is imported separately, each with its own refer-

ence frame, enabling easy repositioning as needed.

  A noteworthy technical consideration in managing a simulation with a sig-

nificant number of imported objects is rendering performance.  For instance,

when the raw Vention table is initially imported, the simulation environment

can achieve a maximum of only 21 FPS, resulting in lagging issues and ren-
